5.title: Inovação aberta: quatro passos para uma corporação criar um CVC
5.content:
inovação aberta : quatro passos para uma corporação criar um cvc 
 no brasil , o mercado de cvc ( corporate venture capital ) tem crescido significativamente nos últimos anos , refletindo o interesse das corporações em se envolver em com o ecossistema de startups e inovação . dados do global corporate venturing institute , revelam que o brasil tem mais de 80 fundos de corporate venture capital ativos , sendo 75 % de les criados nos últimos quatro anos , percentual maior do que a média global , que gira em torno de 40 % . isso por que as corporações brasileiras têm investido em uma variedade de setores e muitas optam por colaborar com aceleradoras ou fundos de venture capital para acessar oportunidades de investimento e compartilhar conhecimento de mercado . 
 investir na criação de um cvc , é uma forma para as corporações terem acesso mais rápido a tecnologias inovadoras , talentos e insights de mercado , ao mesmo tempo em que fornecem às startups financiamento , expertise e potenciais parcerias estratégicas . outro ponto relevante é que o cvc é um recurso para apoiar as empresas de tecnologia a crescerem mais rapidamente e a acess arem recursos que de outra forma não teriam , enquanto permitem que as corporações se mantenham à frente das tendências do setor e que potencialmente podem se tornar disruptivas em seus próprios mercados . 
 para que a tese das companhias tenha sucesso , é preciso considerar alguns pontos estratégicos . o primeiro de les é alinhar o veículo aos objetivos de longo prazo da empresa , complementando sua estratégia de inovação e crescimento . é preciso identificar os setores e tecnologias - chave nos quais a empresa deseja investir e estabelecer metas claras como retorno financeiro , acesso a novas tecnologias ou desenvolvimento de parcerias estratégicas . 
 determinar a estrutura e governança do cvc , incluindo tamanho do fundo , equipe dedicada , processo de tomada de decisão e integração com a empresa - mãe , também é fundamental . para muitas corporaçõ es , esse processo é mais moroso por não saberem por onde começar , por isso muitas empresas têm contratado o serviço de cvc as a service com empresas que já têm uma trajetória neste segmento , para abrir em caminhos para a inovação aberta . 
 outra característica relevante para o avanço da iniciativa é a capacidade de execução ágil e eficiente , aproveitando oportunidades de mercado e respondendo às mudanças no cenário competitivo . testes com provas de conceito , por exemplo , são uma boa forma de retirar impedimentos para a inovação acontecer e para isso , é de extrema importância a busca por parcerias estratégicas com outras empresas de venture capital , aceleradoras , universidades ou instituições de pesquisa para aumentar o acesso a oportunidades de investimento e compartilhar conhecimento e recursos . 
 por fim , é preciso oferecer suporte e recursos adicionais além do financiamento , como mentoria , acesso a redes de contatos , desenvolvimento de negócios e recursos de marketing às startups , como forma de agregar valor . ao considerar esses pontos estratégicos , as corporações podem criar um cvc bem sucedido que impulsione a inovação , promova o crescimento e gere retornos sólidos ao mesmo tempo em que fortaleça sua posição competitiva no mercado . 
 * guilherme amorim é head of innovation services da wayra brasil , cvc da vivo / telefónica , liderando a frente de negócios da organização junto a parceiros estratégicos do grupo , desde 2020 . especialista na jornada de go to market de empresas de tecnologia , guilherme tem quase duas décadas de experiência na construção de estratégias para produtos , serviços e vendas internacionais . foi gestor do programa brasil it + , do governo federal , de fomento à internacionalização de startups , entre 2013 a 2020 . também lider ou atividades de pesquisa e análises de inteligência de mercado para a motorola mobility e atuou em captação de investimentos e fusões e aquisições em consultoria de m & a . foi analista de mercado independente do euromonitor e membro do fórum permanente de micro e pequenas empresas do ministério da economia . o executivo é pós - graduado em negócios internacionais pela universidade mackenzie , especialização em economia , pela fundação getúlio vargas , em fusões e aquisições e private equity & venture capital , pelo insper .

6.title: Corporate Venture Capital - FourWeekMBA
6.content:
corporate venture capital 
 business / by gennaro cuofano / april 17 , 2024 
 corporate venture capital ( cvc ) refers to the investment of corporate funds directly into external startup companies . unlike traditional venture capital firms , which are independent entities , cvc involves established corporations investing in and collaborating with startups to gain strategic advantages , drive innovation , and secure future growth opportunities . 
 by providing capital , expertise , and access to resources , corporate venture capital programs enable corporations to diversify their portfolios , explore new markets , and stay ahead of industry trends . 
 table of contents 
 key principles 
 methodologies and approaches 
 investment strategy 
 due diligence 
 portfolio management 
 benefits of corporate venture capital 
 challenges in implementing corporate venture capital 
 strategies for implementing corporate venture capital 
 real - world examples 
 conclusion 
 related innovation frameworks 
 key principles 
 strategic alignment : corporate venture capital investments are strategically aligned with the core business objectives and long - term goals of the investing corporation . they focus on areas that complement or enhance the corporation ’s existing products , services , or technologies , enabling it to gain a competitive edge in the marketplace . 
 synergistic partnerships : corporate venture capital programs foster synergistic partnerships between established corporations and innovative startups . they leverage the strengths and resources of both parties to accelerate product development , access new markets , and drive mutual growth and success . 
 risk management : corporate venture capital investments involve a degree of risk , but they are often viewed as a strategic means of diversifying risk and exploring new opportunities for growth . by investing in a portfolio of startups across different industries and stages of development , corporations can mitigate risk and maximize potential returns on investment . 
 methodologies and approaches 
 implementing corporate venture capital involves various methodologies and approaches to investment strategy , due diligence , and portfolio management . 
 investment strategy 
 corporate venture capital programs develop investment strategies that align with the corporation ’s overall business objectives and growth priorities . they identify strategic focus areas , market trends , and emerging technologies that offer potential opportunities for investment and collaboration . 
 due diligence 
 corporate venture capital teams conduct thorough due diligence on potential investment opportunities to assess their viability , scalability , and alignment with strategic objectives . they evaluate factors such as market potential , competitive landscape , technology readiness , and management team expertise before making investment decisions . 
 portfolio management 
 corporate venture capital programs actively manage their investment portfolios to maximize returns and strategic value . they monitor the performance of portfolio companies , provide ongoing support and guidance , and seek opportunities for collaboration and synergies with the parent corporation . 
 benefits of corporate venture capital 
 corporate venture capital offers several benefits for corporations seeking to drive innovation , diversify their portfolios , and secure future growth opportunities . 
 access to innovation : corporate venture capital programs provide corporations with access to innovative technologies , business models , and market trends that may not be available through internal r&d efforts . by investing in startups , corporations can tap into external sources of innovation and stay ahead of industry trends . 
 strategic partnerships : corporate venture capital investments facilitate strategic partnerships and collaborations between corporations and startups . they enable corporations to leverage the expertise , resources , and agility of startups to accelerate product development , enter new markets , and drive business growth . 
 diversification : corporate venture capital investments offer corporations a means of diversifying their investment portfolios and reducing reliance on traditional revenue streams . by investing in a portfolio of startups across different industries and sectors , corporations can spread risk and capture opportunities for growth in emerging markets . 
 market insight : corporate venture capital programs provide corporations with valuable insights into market trends , consumer preferences , and competitive dynamics . by closely monitoring the performance of portfolio companies and interacting with entrepreneurs and industry experts , corporations can gain a deeper understanding of emerging opportunities and threats in the marketplace . 
 challenges in implementing corporate venture capital 
 despite its benefits , implementing corporate venture capital can pose several challenges and considerations for corporations . 
 alignment with strategic objectives : corporate venture capital investments must align with the strategic objectives and long - term goals of the investing corporation . ensuring alignment requires careful evaluation of investment opportunities and close coordination between corporate venture capital teams and business units within the corporation . 
 cultural differences : corporate venture capital programs may encounter cultural differences and challenges when collaborating with startups . the corporate culture of established corporations may differ significantly from the entrepreneurial culture of startups , leading to potential conflicts in decision - making , communication , and working styles . 
 resource allocation : corporate venture capital programs require dedicated resources , including financial capital , human capital , and management bandwidth . allocating resources effectively and prioritizing investment opportunities can be challenging , especially in organizations with competing priorities and limited resources . 
 strategies for implementing corporate venture capital 
 to address challenges and maximize the effectiveness of corporate venture capital , corporations can employ various strategies and best practices . 
 strategic alignment : ensure that corporate venture capital investments are aligned with the strategic objectives and growth priorities of the investing corporation . develop clear investment criteria and guidelines that reflect the corporation ’s core competencies , market focus , and long - term goals . 
 partnership development : foster strong partnerships and collaborations between corporate venture capital teams and business units within the corporation . encourage open communication , mutual trust , and shared goals to facilitate effective collaboration and alignment of interests . 
 entrepreneurial engagement : engage with entrepreneurs and startup founders to understand their needs , aspirations , and expectations . provide mentorship , support , and guidance to help startups navigate challenges and leverage opportunities for growth and success . 
 risk management : manage risk effectively by diversifying the corporate venture capital portfolio across different industries , stages of development , and investment sizes . monitor the performance of portfolio companies closely and adjust investment strategies as needed to optimize risk - return profiles . 
 real - world examples 
 corporate venture capital has been successfully implemented by corporations across industries and sectors to drive innovation , foster partnerships , and secure future growth opportunities . 
 google ventures : google ventures , the corporate venture capital arm of alphabet inc. (google ’s parent company ) , invests in startups across a wide range of industries , including technology , healthcare , and consumer products . by leveraging google ’s resources , expertise , and network , google ventures supports startups in scaling their businesses and bringing innovative products to market . 
 intel capital : intel capital , the corporate venture capital arm of intel corporation , focuses on investing in startups developing technologies that complement intel ’s core business areas , such as semiconductor manufacturing , artificial intelligence , and autonomous vehicles . by partnering with intel capital , startups gain access to intel ’s resources , technology expertise , and global network , enabling them to accelerate growth and innovation . 
 samsung ventures : samsung ventures , the corporate venture capital arm of samsung electronics , invests in startups across various sectors , including consumer electronics , software , and healthcare . by leveraging samsung ’s brand , market presence , and distribution channels , samsung ventures helps startups expand their reach and drive innovation in emerging markets . 
 conclusion 
 corporate venture capital is a powerful strategy for corporations seeking to drive innovation , diversify their portfolios , and secure future growth opportunities . by investing in startups and fostering strategic partnerships , corporations can access external sources of innovation , gain market insight , and accelerate product development . despite challenges such as alignment with strategic objectives and cultural differences , corporate venture capital offers significant benefits for corporations looking to stay ahead of industry trends and drive sustainable growth in today ’s dynamic business environment . as corporations continue to explore new avenues for innovation and collaboration , corporate venture capital will remain a key enabler of strategic growth and competitive advantage . 
 related frameworks description when to apply 
 open innovation – a collaborative approach to innovation that involves sharing ideas , resources , and expertise across organizational boundaries to accelerate innovation and drive value creation . open innovation leverages external networks and ecosystems to access diverse perspectives and capabilities . – when seeking to tap into external knowledge and resources for innovation . – embracing open innovation principles to collaborate with partners , customers , and stakeholders , co - create solutions , and access new technologies and markets , accelerating the pace of innovation and enabling corporate venture capital by leveraging collective intelligence and expertise . 
 lean startup methodology – a framework for developing and launching new products or ventures efficiently , using a combination of lean principles , agile practices , and customer validation techniques . the lean startup methodology focuses on building minimum viable products ( mvps ) , testing hypotheses , and learning from customer feedback to iterate and pivot quickly . – when launching new ventures or products with high uncertainty . – applying lean startup principles to validate business ideas , test market assumptions , and iterate on product concepts rapidly , minimizing waste and maximizing learning , which aligns with corporate venture capital ’s emphasis on experimentation and risk - taking . 
 exponential organizations ( exos ) – organizations that leverage exponential technologies , business models , and organizational structures to achieve disproportionate impact and growth . exponential organizations are characterized by attributes such as scalability , agility , and innovation . – when designing or transforming organizations for exponential growth . – studying exponential organizations ’ characteristics and practices to understand how to harness disruptive technologies , leverage network effects , and foster a culture of innovation and experimentation , aligning with corporate venture capital ’s ambition to drive transformative impact and scale rapidly . 
 business model canvas – a strategic management tool that provides a visual framework for describing , analyzing , and designing business models . the business model canvas consists of nine building blocks that represent key aspects of a business , including value proposition , customer segments , and revenue streams . – when developing or evaluating business models for new ventures . – using the business model canvas to map out key components of a business model , identify opportunities for innovation , and test assumptions , guiding investment decisions and strategic planning processes in corporate venture capital initiatives . 
 portfolio management – involves the strategic allocation of resources and management of investments across a portfolio of ventures or projects to optimize risk - return profiles and achieve strategic objectives . portfolio management helps organizations diversify risk , maximize value , and align investments with corporate goals . – when managing a portfolio of investments in startups or ventures . – applying portfolio management principles and techniques to assess investment opportunities , allocate resources effectively , monitor performance , and make informed decisions about portfolio composition and strategy , supporting corporate venture capital initiatives and maximizing value creation . 
 strategic partnerships – collaborative relationships between corporations and external entities , such as startups , universities , or research institutions , to access complementary capabilities , technologies , or markets . strategic partnerships enable corporations to enhance innovation , accelerate growth , and drive competitive advantage . – when seeking to leverage external expertise and resources for innovation . – establishing strategic partnerships with startups , academic institutions , or industry collaborators to access emerging technologies , co - develop solutions , and explore new market opportunities , enhancing corporate venture capital initiatives and fostering a culture of innovation and collaboration . 
 corporate accelerators – programs launched by corporations to support and accelerate the growth of startups through mentorship , resources , and access to networks . corporate accelerators provide startups with funding , expertise , and market opportunities while enabling corporations to gain strategic insights and access to innovation . – when seeking to engage with startups and drive innovation internally . – launching corporate accelerator programs to invest in and support startups aligned with corporate strategic priorities , fostering entrepreneurship , and driving innovation internally while gaining exposure to emerging technologies and business models through corporate venture capital initiatives . 
 corporate incubators – initiatives launched by corporations to nurture and develop new ventures or business ideas internally . corporate incubators provide resources , support , and infrastructure to employees or external entrepreneurs to explore and develop innovative concepts . – when fostering a culture of entrepreneurship and innovation internally . – establishing corporate incubators to encourage employees to explore new business ideas , develop innovative solutions , and validate market opportunities , supporting corporate venture capital initiatives and driving intrapreneurship within the organization . 
 corporate innovation labs – dedicated units within corporations focused on research , development , and experimentation with emerging technologies and business models . corporate innovation labs drive innovation by exploring new opportunities , prototyping solutions , and validating market demand . – when investing in research and development of new technologies or solutions . – establishing corporate innovation labs to explore emerging trends , experiment with new technologies , and develop innovative solutions that align with corporate strategic priorities , driving corporate venture capital initiatives and fostering a culture of innovation and experimentation within the organization . 
 technology scouting – a systematic process of identifying , evaluating , and acquiring external technologies or innovations that complement or enhance corporate capabilities and strategic objectives . technology scouting helps corporations stay abreast of industry trends and emerging technologies . – when seeking to access external technologies for strategic purposes . – implementing technology scouting programs to identify promising startups , technologies , or intellectual property that align with corporate strategic priorities , supporting corporate venture capital initiatives and driving innovation and competitive advantage within the organization . 
 related innovation frameworks 
 business engineering 
 business model innovation 
 business model innovation is about increasing the success of an organization with existing products and technologies by crafting a compelling value proposition able to propel a new business model to scale up customers and create a lasting competitive advantage . and it all starts by mastering the key customers . 
 innovation theory 
 the innovation loop is a methodology / framework derived from the bell labs , which produced innovation at scale throughout the 20th century . they learned how to leverage a hybrid innovation management model based on science , invention , engineering , and manufacturing at scale . by leveraging individual genius , creativity , and small / large groups . 
 types of innovation 
 according to how well defined is the problem and how well defined the domain , we have four main types of innovations : basic research ( problem and domain or not well defined ) ; breakthrough innovation ( domain is not well defined , the problem is well defined ) ; sustaining innovation ( both problem and domain are well defined ) ; and disruptive innovation ( domain is well defined , the problem is not well defined ) . 
 continuous innovation 
 that is a process that requires a continuous feedback loop to develop a valuable product and build a viable business model . continuous innovation is a mindset where products and services are designed and delivered to tune them around the customers ’ problem and not the technical solution of its founders . 
 disruptive innovation 
 disruptive innovation as a term was first described by clayton m. christensen , an american academic and business consultant whom the economist called “ the most influential management thinker of his time . ” disruptive innovation describes the process by which a product or service takes hold at the bottom of a market and eventually displaces established competitors , products , firms , or alliances . 
 business competition 
 in a business world driven by technology and digitalization , competition is much more fluid , as innovation becomes a bottom-up approach that can come from anywhere . thus , making it much harder to define the boundaries of existing markets . therefore , a proper business competition analysis looks at customer , technology , distribution , and financial model overlaps . while at the same time looking at future potential intersections among industries that in the short - term seem unrelated . 
 technological modeling 
 technological modeling is a discipline to provide the basis for companies to sustain innovation , thus developing incremental products . while also looking at breakthrough innovative products that can pave the way for long - term success . in a sort of barbell strategy , technological modeling suggests having a two - sided approach , on the one hand , to keep sustaining continuous innovation as a core part of the business model . on the other hand , it places bets on future developments that have the potential to break through and take a leap forward . 
 diffusion of innovation 
 sociologist e.m rogers developed the diffusion of innovation theory in 1962 with the premise that with enough time , tech products are adopted by wider society as a whole . people adopting those technologies are divided according to their psychologic profiles in five groups : innovators , early adopters , early majority , late majority , and laggards . 
 frugal innovation 
 in the ted talk entitled “ creative problem - solving in the face of extreme limits ” navi radjou defined frugal innovation as “ the ability to create more economic and social value using fewer resources . frugal innovation is not about making do ; it ’s about making things better . ” indian people call it jugaad , a hindi word that means finding inexpensive solutions based on existing scarce resources to solve problems smartly . 
 constructive disruption 
 a consumer brand company like procter & gamble ( p & g ) defines “ constructive disruption ” as : a willingness to change , adapt , and create new trends and technologies that will shape our industry for the future . according to p & g , it moves around four pillars : lean innovation , brand building , supply chain , and digitalization & data analytics . 
 growth matrix 
 in the fourweekmba growth matrix , you can apply growth for existing customers by tackling the same problems ( gain mode ) . or by tackling existing problems , for new customers ( expand mode ) . or by tackling new problems for existing customers ( extend mode ) . or perhaps by tackling whole new problems for new customers ( reinvent mode ) . 
 innovation funnel 
 an innovation funnel is a tool or process ensuring only the best ideas are executed . in a metaphorical sense , the funnel screens innovative ideas for viability so that only the best products , processes , or business models are launched to the market . an innovation funnel provides a framework for the screening and testing of innovative ideas for viability . 
 idea generation 
 design thinking 
 tim brown , executive chair of ideo , defined design thinking as “ a human - centered approach to innovation that draws from the designer ’s toolkit to integrate the needs of people , the possibilities of technology , and the requirements for business success . ” therefore , desirability , feasibility , and viability are balanced to solve critical problems .

 corporate venturing design : how to design and structure your corporate venturing projects and programs 
 1. introduction to corporate venturing 
 corporate venturing is a strategic approach that enables established corporations to leverage the innovation potential of startups and entrepreneurs . by collaborating with external partners , corporations can access new markets , technologies , capabilities , and business models that can enhance their competitive advantage and growth prospects . corporate venturing can take various forms , such as corporate venture capital , corporate incubators and accelerators , corporate innovation labs , strategic partnerships , and acquisitions . each form has its own benefits and challenges , and requires a different level of commitment and involvement from the corporation . in this section , we will explore the following aspects of corporate venturing : 
 1. why do corporations engage in corporate venturing ? corporations have different motivations and objectives for pursuing corporate venturing . some of the common reasons are : 
 - to innovate faster and cheaper by tapping into the creativity , agility , and risk - taking culture of startups and entrepreneurs . 
 - to diversify their portfolio and explore new opportunities beyond their core business domains and competencies . 
 - to learn from the best practices and emerging trends in the startup ecosystem and adopt them in their own operations and processes . 
 - to build relationships and networks with potential partners , customers , suppliers , and talent in the innovation community . 
 - to enhance their reputation and brand image as an innovative and forward - looking organization . 
 2. what are the benefits and challenges of corporate venturing ? corporate venturing can offer significant advantages for corporations , such as : 
 - increased innovation output and performance by accessing novel ideas , solutions , and technologies that can improve their products , services , and processes . 
 - reduced innovation costs and risks by sharing the financial and operational burden of innovation with external partners and leveraging their expertise and resources . 
 - expanded market reach and customer base by entering new segments , regions , and industries that are served by the startups and entrepreneurs . 
 - enhanced organizational capabilities and culture by acquiring new skills , knowledge , and mindsets that can foster a more entrepreneurial and collaborative environment within the corporation . 
 - improved strategic positioning and competitiveness by gaining a first - mover advantage or a stronger foothold in the emerging and disruptive markets and technologies . 
 however , corporate venturing also poses some challenges and difficulties for corporations , such as : 
 - aligning the goals and expectations of the internal and external stakeholders involved in the corporate venturing activities and ensuring a clear and consistent communication and feedback mechanism . 
 - balancing the autonomy and control of the startups and entrepreneurs and providing them with the appropriate level of support and guidance without stifling their creativity and independence . 
 - integrating the innovations and learnings from the corporate venturing initiatives into the core business and operations of the corporation and overcoming the potential resistance and inertia from the existing culture and systems . 
 - measuring the impact and value of the corporate venturing outcomes and assessing the return on investment and the long - term strategic implications . 
 3. how to design and structure corporate venturing projects and programs ? there is no one - size - fits - all approach to corporate venturing , as each corporation has its own vision , strategy , resources , and capabilities . however , some of the key elements and steps that can help corporations design and structure their corporate venturing projects and programs are : 
 - define the scope and objectives of the corporate venturing activities and align them with the overall corporate strategy and vision . 
 - identify the target domains and segments of interest and relevance for the corporation and conduct a market and technology analysis to understand the current and future trends and opportunities . 
 - select the most suitable form and mode of corporate venturing that matches the corporation 's goals , capabilities , and resources and fits the nature and stage of the startups and entrepreneurs . 
 - establish the governance and management structure and processes for the corporate venturing activities and assign the roles and responsibilities of the internal and external actors and stakeholders . 
 - implement and execute the corporate venturing activities and monitor and evaluate the progress and performance of the startups and entrepreneurs and the corporation 's involvement and contribution . 
 - review and refine the corporate venturing activities and outcomes and capture and disseminate the learnings and best practices within and outside the corporation . 
 an example of a successful corporate venturing project is the collaboration between google and magic leap , a startup that develops augmented reality technology . google invested $ 542 million in magic leap in 2014 and became its largest shareholder . google also provided strategic and technical support and guidance to magic leap and helped it develop its product and market strategy . in return , google gained access to magic leap 's cutting - edge technology and expertise and enhanced its position in the emerging field of augmented reality . google also learned from magic leap 's innovative and experimental culture and applied some of its principles and practices in its own organization .

 2. benefits of corporate venturing 
 benefits of corporate venturing 
 corporate venturing is a strategic approach that allows established companies to collaborate with startups , entrepreneurs , and innovators to create new value , explore new markets , and foster innovation . corporate venturing can take various forms , such as corporate venture capital , incubators , accelerators , partnerships , joint ventures , spin - offs , and acquisitions . by engaging in corporate venturing , companies can gain several benefits , such as : 
 1. access to external innovation : corporate venturing enables companies to tap into the creativity , agility , and expertise of startups and entrepreneurs , who often have novel solutions , technologies , and business models that can complement or disrupt the existing offerings of the company . for example , google acquired youtube in 2006 to enhance its video platform and leverage the user - generated content of the popular startup . 
 2. enhance core competencies : corporate venturing can help companies strengthen their core capabilities and competencies by learning from the best practices , insights , and feedback of their venture partners . for example , procter & gamble partnered with connect + develop , an open innovation platform , to source ideas and solutions from external innovators , which helped the company improve its product development , marketing , and distribution processes . 
 3. diversify revenue streams : corporate venturing can help companies generate new sources of income and growth by entering new markets , segments , or geographies , or by creating new products , services , or business models . for example , amazon launched amazon web services ( aws ) in 2006 as a spin-off from its e-commerce business , which became a leading provider of cloud computing services and a major contributor to amazon 's revenue and profitability . 
 4. mitigate risks : corporate venturing can help companies reduce the uncertainty and risks associated with innovation by sharing the costs , resources , and responsibilities with their venture partners . for example , bmw formed a joint venture with toyota in 2013 to co - develop hydrogen fuel cell technology , which allowed both companies to leverage their respective strengths and expertise , while spreading the risks and investments of developing a new technology . 
 5. build a culture of innovation : corporate venturing can help companies foster a culture of innovation within their organization by exposing their employees , managers , and leaders to new ideas , perspectives , and opportunities . corporate venturing can also help companies attract and retain talent , as well as enhance their reputation and brand image as an innovative and forward - looking company . for example , coca-cola launched the founders program in 2013 , which invited entrepreneurs to co - create new ventures with the company , which provided them with funding , mentorship , and access to coca-cola 's network and assets . the program also helped coca-cola cultivate an entrepreneurial mindset and culture among its employees .

 3. key elements of corporate venturing design 
 corporate venturing design is the process of creating and managing strategic partnerships between established corporations and innovative startups . it can take various forms , such as corporate venture capital , incubators , accelerators , joint ventures , licensing , and acquisitions . the main benefits of corporate venturing are accessing new technologies , markets , and talent , enhancing innovation capabilities , and generating financial returns . however , corporate venturing also involves significant challenges , such as aligning objectives , managing conflicts , and balancing risks and rewards . therefore , it is crucial to design and structure corporate venturing projects and programs carefully and systematically . in this section , we will discuss some of the key elements of corporate venturing design , such as : 
 1. objectives and metrics : the first step in corporate venturing design is to define the objectives and metrics of the corporate venturing activities . these should be aligned with the overall corporate strategy and vision , as well as the specific needs and opportunities of the business units and functions . the objectives and metrics should also be clear , measurable , and realistic , and reflect both the short - term and long - term outcomes of corporate venturing . for example , some possible objectives and metrics are : increasing revenue growth , enhancing customer satisfaction , improving operational efficiency , expanding into new markets , acquiring new capabilities , fostering a culture of innovation , and generating positive returns on investment . 
 2. governance and organization : the second step in corporate venturing design is to establish the governance and organization of the corporate venturing activities . this involves deciding who will be responsible for initiating , approving , executing , and monitoring the corporate venturing projects and programs , and how they will communicate and coordinate with each other . the governance and organization should also ensure that there is a balance between centralization and decentralization , autonomy and control , and flexibility and accountability . for example , some possible governance and organization models are : a dedicated corporate venturing unit , a network of corporate venturing champions , a hybrid of centralized and decentralized teams , and a matrix of functional and business unit representatives . 
 3. selection and evaluation : the third step in corporate venturing design is to select and evaluate the potential corporate venturing partners and opportunities . this involves screening and sourcing the startups that match the corporate venturing objectives and criteria , and conducting due diligence and valuation to assess their fit , feasibility , and attractiveness . the selection and evaluation should also consider the different types and stages of corporate venturing , such as seed , early , growth , and late stage , and the different modes and mechanisms of corporate venturing , such as equity , debt , grants , and contracts . for example , some possible selection and evaluation methods are : scouting and scouting platforms , referrals and recommendations , competitions and challenges , and data and analytics . 
 4. engagement and integration : the fourth step in corporate venturing design is to engage and integrate the selected corporate venturing partners and opportunities . this involves negotiating and structuring the terms and conditions of the corporate venturing deal , and implementing and managing the corporate venturing relationship . the engagement and integration should also address the potential issues and risks of corporate venturing , such as cultural and operational differences , intellectual property and confidentiality , governance and decision making , and performance and exit . for example , some possible engagement and integration practices are : co-creation and co - development , mentoring and coaching , networking and exposure , and monitoring and feedback . 
 these are some of the key elements of corporate venturing design that can help corporations and startups to create and sustain successful and mutually beneficial partnerships . by following these steps , corporations can leverage the innovation potential of startups , and startups can access the resources and capabilities of corporations . corporate venturing design is not a one - size - fits - all approach , but rather a dynamic and iterative process that requires constant adaptation and learning . therefore , corporations and startups should always be open to experimenting and improving their corporate venturing design and structure .

 4. defining objectives and goals 
 defining your objectives 
 objectives and goals 
 in this section , we delve into the crucial aspect of defining objectives and goals for corporate venturing projects and programs . by clearly outlining the desired outcomes , organizations can align their efforts and resources effectively . let 's explore this topic from various perspectives : 
 1. understand the purpose : before embarking on any corporate venturing initiative , it is essential to identify the purpose behind it . this could include expanding into new markets , fostering innovation , or driving strategic partnerships . by clarifying the purpose , organizations can set specific objectives that align with their overall business strategy . 
 2. set smart goals : smart goals are specific , measurable , achievable , relevant , and time - bound . they provide a clear framework for defining objectives and tracking progress . for example , a smart goal could be to achieve a 20 % increase in market share within the next two years through strategic collaborations and product innovation . 
 3. consider stakeholder perspectives : when defining objectives and goals , it is crucial to consider the perspectives of various stakeholders . this includes internal stakeholders such as executives , employees , and shareholders , as well as external stakeholders like customers , partners , and investors . by understanding their needs and expectations , organizations can ensure that their objectives are aligned with stakeholder interests . 
 4. prioritize key metrics : to measure the success of corporate venturing projects , it is important to identify key metrics that reflect progress towards the defined objectives . these metrics could include financial indicators ( e . g . , revenue growth , return on investment ) , operational metrics ( e . g . , time to market , cost savings ) , or strategic metrics ( e . g . , market share , brand perception ) . by tracking these metrics , organizations can assess the effectiveness of their initiatives and make data - driven decisions . 
 5. foster a culture of innovation : objectives and goals should also reflect the organization 's commitment to fostering a culture of innovation . this could involve encouraging employees to generate new ideas , promoting cross - functional collaboration , and investing in research and development . by aligning objectives with innovation , organizations can drive continuous improvement and stay ahead in a rapidly evolving business landscape . 
 defining objectives and goals - corporate venturing design : how to design and structure your corporate venturing projects and programs 
 5. structuring corporate venturing projects 
 one of the most important aspects of corporate venturing is how to structure the projects and programs that aim to create new value for the organization . structuring corporate venturing projects involves defining the scope , objectives , resources , governance , and evaluation criteria of each initiative . it also involves aligning the projects with the strategic goals and vision of the organization , as well as the needs and expectations of the stakeholders . in this section , we will discuss some of the best practices and challenges of structuring corporate venturing projects , and provide some examples of successful cases . 
 some of the key points to consider when structuring corporate venturing projects are : 
 1. choose the right type of project . depending on the level of innovation , risk , and uncertainty involved , corporate venturing projects can be classified into different types , such as incremental , radical , disruptive , or exploratory . each type of project requires a different approach , mindset , and skillset from the team members , managers , and sponsors . for example , incremental projects aim to improve existing products or services , while disruptive projects aim to create new markets or business models . choosing the right type of project can help to set realistic expectations , allocate appropriate resources , and measure the outcomes . 
 2. define the project scope and objectives . a clear and specific definition of the project scope and objectives can help to guide the team 's actions and decisions , and avoid scope creep or mission drift . the project scope should describe what the project will and will not do , and the project objectives should describe what the project aims to achieve and how it will be measured . the project scope and objectives should be aligned with the organization 's strategic goals and vision , and should be communicated to all the stakeholders involved . 
 3. select the right team and resources . the success of a corporate venturing project depends largely on the quality and diversity of the team and the resources available . the team should consist of people with different backgrounds , skills , and perspectives , who can collaborate effectively and creatively . the team should also have a clear leader , who can provide direction , motivation , and feedback . the resources should include financial , human , and physical assets , as well as access to external networks , partners , and mentors . the team and resources should be allocated according to the needs and challenges of the project , and should be flexible and adaptable to changes . 
 4. establish the project governance and accountability . a well - defined and transparent project governance and accountability system can help to ensure the smooth and efficient execution of the project , and to manage the risks and uncertainties involved . the project governance should specify the roles and responsibilities of the team members , managers , and sponsors , as well as the decision - making and reporting processes . the project accountability should specify the performance indicators and evaluation criteria of the project , as well as the rewards and incentives for the team . the project governance and accountability should be consistent with the organization 's culture and values , and should be reviewed and updated regularly . 
 5. learn and iterate . one of the main characteristics of corporate venturing projects is that they involve a high degree of experimentation and learning . the team should adopt a lean and agile methodology , which involves testing and validating the assumptions and hypotheses of the project , and iterating and pivoting based on the feedback and results . the team should also document and share the learnings and insights from the project , and apply them to future projects or programs . the team should also celebrate the successes and failures of the project , and recognize the efforts and contributions of the team members . 
 some examples of corporate venturing projects that have been structured effectively are : 
 - google x. google x is a research and development facility that works on " moonshot " projects that aim to solve big and audacious problems using breakthrough technology . some of the projects that have emerged from google x include self - driving cars , smart contact lenses , balloon - powered internet , and delivery drones . google x follows a rigorous and systematic process to structure its projects , which involves defining the problem , the solution , and the breakthrough ; prototyping and testing the solution ; and scaling and launching the solution . 
 - bmw startup garage . bmw startup garage is a program that allows bmw to collaborate with startups that have innovative solutions for the automotive industry . the program involves selecting and inviting startups to work with bmw for four months , during which they receive access to bmw 's resources , network , and expertise . the program also involves validating and integrating the startups ' solutions into bmw 's products or services , and establishing long - term partnerships or investments with the startups . 
 - unilever foundry . unilever foundry is a platform that connects unilever with startups that have solutions for the consumer goods industry . the platform involves sourcing and screening startups that match unilever 's needs and challenges , and providing them with opportunities to pilot their solutions with unilever 's brands or functions . the platform also involves mentoring and supporting the startups , and scaling and integrating their solutions into unilever 's business .

 6. identifying and evaluating potential partnerships 
 identifying and evaluating the potential 
 potential partnerships 
 one of the key aspects of corporate venturing is finding and collaborating with external partners who can provide complementary resources , capabilities , and insights to the corporate venture . however , identifying and evaluating potential partnerships is not a trivial task . it requires a clear understanding of the venture 's objectives , value proposition , and needs , as well as a systematic approach to screening , assessing , and engaging with potential partners . in this section , we will discuss some of the best practices and frameworks for identifying and evaluating potential partnerships for corporate venturing projects and programs . we will also provide some examples of successful partnerships that have enabled corporate ventures to achieve their goals and create value for both parties . 
 some of the steps involved in identifying and evaluating potential partnerships are : 
 1. define the criteria and objectives for the partnership . before looking for potential partners , it is important to have a clear idea of what the venture wants to achieve and what kind of partner it needs . some of the criteria and objectives that can be used to define the partnership are : 
 - the strategic fit : how well does the partner align with the venture 's vision , mission , and goals ? how can the partner help the venture achieve its strategic objectives and create competitive advantage ? 
 - the value proposition : what value can the partner offer to the venture and vice versa ? how can the partner enhance the venture 's product , service , or solution ? how can the venture add value to the partner 's business or customer base ? 
 - the resource complementarity : what resources , capabilities , and assets can the partner provide to the venture and vice versa ? how can the partner fill the gaps or weaknesses of the venture ? how can the venture leverage the strengths or opportunities of the partner ? 
 - the cultural compatibility : how compatible are the partner 's and the venture 's organizational cultures , values , and norms ? how well can the partner and the venture communicate , collaborate , and trust each other ? how can the partner and the venture manage potential conflicts or disagreements ? 
 2. identify and screen potential partners . once the criteria and objectives for the partnership are defined , the next step is to identify and screen potential partners who meet those criteria and objectives . some of the sources and methods that can be used to identify and screen potential partners are : 
 - internal sources : the venture can leverage its own network and contacts within the corporate parent or other business units to find potential partners who have existing relationships or collaborations with the corporation . the venture can also use internal databases , reports , or newsletters to identify potential partners who have relevant expertise , experience , or reputation in the industry or domain of interest . 
 - external sources : the venture can use external sources such as industry associations , trade shows , conferences , events , publications , or online platforms to find potential partners who have exposure or presence in the industry or domain of interest . the venture can also use external databases , directories , or search engines to find potential partners who have specific attributes , characteristics , or credentials that match the venture 's needs . 
 - referrals and recommendations : the venture can ask for referrals and recommendations from its customers , suppliers , advisors , mentors , investors , or other stakeholders who have connections or insights into the industry or domain of interest . the venture can also use social media , online forums , or communities to solicit referrals and recommendations from peers , experts , or influencers who have knowledge or experience in the industry or domain of interest . 
 - screening tools and frameworks : the venture can use screening tools and frameworks such as swot analysis , pestel analysis , porter 's five forces analysis , or value chain analysis to evaluate the potential partners based on their strengths , weaknesses , opportunities , threats , political , economic , social , technological , environmental , legal , competitive , or value - adding factors . the venture can also use screening tools and frameworks such as the partner fit matrix , the partner attractiveness matrix , or the partner compatibility matrix to compare and rank the potential partners based on their strategic fit , value proposition , resource complementarity , or cultural compatibility with the venture . 
 3. assess and select the best partner . after identifying and screening potential partners , the final step is to assess and select the best partner for the venture . some of the activities and methods that can be used to assess and select the best partner are : 
 - due diligence : the venture can conduct due diligence on the potential partner to verify the accuracy and validity of the information and data provided by the partner . the venture can also conduct due diligence on the potential partner to identify and evaluate the risks and challenges associated with the partnership . the due diligence can cover aspects such as the partner 's financial performance , legal status , operational efficiency , customer satisfaction , innovation capability , or ethical standards . 
 - negotiation : the venture can negotiate with the potential partner to reach a mutually beneficial and satisfactory agreement on the terms and conditions of the partnership . the negotiation can cover aspects such as the roles and responsibilities , the expectations and deliverables , the resources and contributions , the governance and decision - making , the communication and coordination , the performance and evaluation , or the rewards and incentives of the partnership . 
 - pilot or trial : the venture can conduct a pilot or trial with the potential partner to test and validate the feasibility and viability of the partnership . the pilot or trial can involve launching a prototype , a minimum viable product , or a pilot project with the partner to measure and evaluate the outcomes and impacts of the partnership . the pilot or trial can also involve soliciting and incorporating feedback from the partner , the customers , or other stakeholders to improve and optimize the partnership . 
 - formalization : the venture can formalize the partnership with the best partner by signing a contract or a memorandum of understanding that specifies and documents the details and agreements of the partnership . the formalization can also involve announcing and communicating the partnership to the internal and external audiences to generate awareness and support for the partnership . 
 some examples of successful partnerships that have enabled corporate ventures to achieve their goals and create value for both parties are : 
 - google and nasa : google and nasa partnered to create google earth , a web - based platform that allows users to explore and visualize the earth and other planets using satellite imagery , maps , terrain , and 3d buildings . the partnership enabled google to access nasa 's data and expertise in space exploration and geospatial technology , and enabled nasa to reach a wider and more diverse audience and promote its scientific and educational missions . 
 - starbucks and spotify : starbucks and spotify partnered to create starbucks music , a digital music service that allows starbucks customers to discover and enjoy curated playlists and songs from starbucks stores and baristas using the starbucks app and spotify app . the partnership enabled starbucks to enhance its customer experience and loyalty by offering personalized and engaging music content , and enabled spotify to expand its user base and exposure by leveraging starbucks ' global network and brand . 
 - bmw and daimler : bmw and daimler partnered to create your now , a joint venture that offers mobility services such as car - sharing , ride - hailing , parking , charging , and multimodal transportation using a single app and platform . the partnership enabled bmw and daimler to combine their resources and capabilities to compete and innovate in the rapidly changing and growing mobility market , and enabled customers to access a variety of convenient and sustainable mobility options .

 7. implementing and managing corporate venturing programs 
 implementing and managing 
 corporate venturing is a strategic approach to innovation that involves creating , investing in , or partnering with external ventures that can provide new sources of growth , competitive advantage , or value creation for the corporation . however , corporate venturing is not a one - size - fits - all solution . different types of corporate venturing projects and programs require different levels of involvement , resources , governance , and evaluation from the corporation . therefore , implementing and managing corporate venturing programs is a complex and dynamic process that requires careful planning , execution , and adaptation . in this section , we will discuss some of the key aspects and best practices of implementing and managing corporate venturing programs , such as : 
 1. defining the objectives and scope of the program . before launching a corporate venturing program , the corporation should have a clear vision of what it wants to achieve and how it aligns with its overall strategy , culture , and capabilities . the objectives and scope of the program should be specific , measurable , achievable , relevant , and time - bound ( smart ) , and should reflect the type and stage of the ventures that the corporation is interested in . for example , some corporations may focus on early - stage ventures that can offer disruptive innovations , while others may prefer later - stage ventures that can provide incremental improvements or synergies . the objectives and scope of the program should also consider the potential risks , challenges , and trade - offs involved in corporate venturing , such as the balance between exploration and exploitation , autonomy and control , and short - term and long - term returns . 
 2. selecting the appropriate mode and mechanism of corporate venturing . depending on the objectives and scope of the program , the corporation should choose the most suitable mode and mechanism of corporate venturing that can deliver the desired outcomes and benefits . the mode of corporate venturing refers to the degree of integration and separation between the corporation and the ventures , while the mechanism of corporate venturing refers to the specific form and structure of the relationship . there are various modes and mechanisms of corporate venturing , such as corporate incubators , accelerators , venture studios , 
 venture capital 
 , corporate venture capital , strategic partnerships , joint ventures , mergers and acquisitions , and spin - offs . each mode and mechanism has its own advantages and disadvantages , and requires different levels of commitment , investment , involvement , and governance from the corporation . for example , corporate incubators and accelerators can provide more support and guidance to the ventures , but may also impose more restrictions and constraints , while venture capital and corporate venture capital can offer more flexibility and independence to the ventures , but may also entail more uncertainty and competition . the corporation should evaluate the pros and cons of each mode and mechanism , and select the one that best fits its objectives , capabilities , and culture . 
 3. establishing the roles and responsibilities of the program team and stakeholders . implementing and managing a corporate venturing program requires a dedicated and cross - functional team that can oversee and coordinate the various activities and processes involved in the program . the team should consist of members with diverse backgrounds , skills , and perspectives , such as business , technology , finance , legal , and innovation . the team should also have a clear leader who can provide direction , guidance , and support to the team and the ventures , and who can communicate and collaborate effectively with the internal and external stakeholders of the program . the stakeholders of the program may include the senior management , the business units , the r&d units , the customers , the suppliers , the regulators , and the industry associations . the roles and responsibilities of the team and the stakeholders should be clearly defined and agreed upon , and should be aligned with the objectives and scope of the program . the team and the stakeholders should also establish regular and transparent communication channels , feedback mechanisms , and reporting systems , to ensure that the program is running smoothly and effectively , and that any issues or conflicts are resolved promptly and constructively . 
 4. developing and applying the criteria and methods for selecting and evaluating the ventures . one of the most critical and challenging aspects of implementing and managing a corporate venturing program is selecting and evaluating the ventures that the corporation will engage with . the corporation should develop and apply a set of criteria and methods that can help it identify , screen , and assess the potential and performance of the ventures , and that can match the corporation 's objectives and expectations . the criteria and methods should be based on both quantitative and qualitative factors , such as the market opportunity , the value proposition , the competitive advantage , the innovation potential , the financial viability , the strategic fit , the cultural fit , and the social and environmental impact of the ventures . the corporation should also use a variety of sources and tools to collect and analyze the data and information about the ventures , such as 
 market research 
 , customer feedback , expert opinions , due diligence , financial modeling , and portfolio analysis . the corporation should apply the criteria and methods consistently and objectively , and should also be open to learning and adapting them as the program progresses and the context changes . 
 5. providing the appropriate level and type of support and resources to the ventures . another key aspect of implementing and managing a corporate venturing program is providing the appropriate level and type of support and resources to the ventures that the corporation has selected and engaged with . the support and resources may include financial , technical , operational , strategic , and relational aspects , such as funding , equipment , facilities , mentorship , coaching , training , networking , access to customers , markets , suppliers , and partners , and endorsement and recognition . the level and type of support and resources should be tailored to the specific needs and goals of each venture , and should also reflect the mode and mechanism of corporate venturing that the corporation has chosen . the corporation should monitor and measure the impact and value of the support and resources that it provides to the ventures , and should also solicit and incorporate the feedback and suggestions from the ventures on how to improve and optimize them . the corporation should also balance the support and resources that it provides to the ventures with the expectations and obligations that it sets for them , such as the milestones , deliverables , kpis , and reporting requirements . 
 6. managing the relationship and interaction between the corporation and the ventures . the final aspect of implementing and managing a corporate venturing program is managing the relationship and interaction between the corporation and the ventures that it has selected , engaged , and supported . the relationship and interaction between the corporation and the ventures can be influenced by various factors , such as the mode and mechanism of corporate venturing , the objectives and scope of the program , the roles and responsibilities of the team and the stakeholders , the criteria and methods for selecting and evaluating the ventures , and the level and type of support and resources provided to the ventures . the relationship and interaction between the corporation and the ventures can also evolve and change over time , as the program progresses and the context changes . the corporation should strive to maintain a positive , constructive , and collaborative relationship and interaction with the ventures , and should also foster a culture of trust , respect , and mutual learning and benefit . the corporation should also manage the potential tensions and conflicts that may arise between the corporation and the ventures , or among the ventures themselves , and should seek to resolve them in a fair and timely manner . the corporation should also be prepared to deal with the possible outcomes and scenarios of the relationship and interaction with the ventures , such as the continuation , expansion , reduction , termination , or exit of the relationship and interaction , and should plan and execute them accordingly . 
 8. measuring success and return on investment 
 one of the most important aspects of corporate venturing is to measure the success and return on investment ( roi ) of the projects and programs . this is not only essential for evaluating the performance and impact of the venturing activities , but also for communicating the value and benefits to the internal and external stakeholders . however , measuring success and roi in corporate venturing is not a straightforward task , as there are many challenges and complexities involved . in this section , we will discuss some of the key issues and best practices for measuring success and roi in corporate venturing , from different perspectives and dimensions . we will also provide some examples of how some leading companies have approached this topic in their venturing initiatives . 
 some of the main points to consider when measuring success and roi in corporate venturing are : 
 1. define the objectives and metrics of success . the first step is to clearly define the objectives and goals of the corporate venturing projects and programs , and align them with the overall corporate strategy and vision . this will help to establish the criteria and indicators of success , and to select the appropriate metrics and methods to measure them . depending on the type and stage of the venturing activities , the objectives and metrics of success may vary . for example , some common objectives and metrics of success for corporate venturing are : 
 - innovation : the number and quality of new ideas , products , services , or business models generated or adopted through the venturing activities . 
 - growth : the increase in revenue , market share , customer base , or competitive advantage resulting from the venturing activities . 
 - learning : the acquisition of new knowledge , skills , capabilities , or insights through the venturing activities . 
 - collaboration : the extent and quality of the relationships and partnerships established or strengthened through the venturing activities , both internally and externally . 
 - impact : the contribution of the venturing activities to the social , environmental , or economic well - being of the stakeholders and the society at large . 
 2. choose the appropriate methods and tools to measure success and roi . the second step is to choose the most suitable methods and tools to measure the success and roi of the corporate venturing projects and programs , based on the objectives and metrics defined in the previous step . there are various methods and tools available for measuring success and roi in corporate venturing , ranging from qualitative to quantitative , and from financial to non - financial . some of the most common methods and tools are : 
 - surveys and interviews : these are useful for collecting feedback and opinions from the participants and beneficiaries of the venturing activities , such as the employees , customers , partners , or investors . they can help to assess the satisfaction , engagement , motivation , or perception of the venturing activities , and to identify the strengths , weaknesses , opportunities , or threats . 
 - case studies and stories : these are effective for capturing and showcasing the outcomes and impacts of the venturing activities , in terms of the innovation , growth , learning , or collaboration achieved . they can help to illustrate the challenges , solutions , lessons learned , or best practices of the venturing activities , and to inspire and influence the stakeholders and the audience . 
 - dashboards and scorecards : these are convenient for tracking and reporting the progress and performance of the venturing activities , in terms of the metrics and indicators of success . they can help to monitor and compare the results and achievements of the venturing activities , and to identify the gaps , risks , or areas for improvement . 
 - models and formulas : these are helpful for calculating and estimating the roi of the venturing activities , in terms of the financial returns or benefits . they can help to measure and justify the investment and expenditure of the venturing activities , and to evaluate the efficiency and effectiveness of the venturing activities . some examples of models and formulas for measuring roi in corporate venturing are : 
 - net present value ( npv ) : this is the difference between the present value of the cash inflows and the present value of the cash outflows of the venturing activities , discounted by a certain rate . it measures the profitability of the venturing activities , and indicates whether they add value to the company or not . a positive npv means that the venturing activities are profitable , while a negative npv means that they are not . 
 - internal rate of return ( irr ) : this is the discount rate that makes the npv of the venturing activities equal to zero . it measures the annualized return of the venturing activities , and indicates how well they perform compared to other investment alternatives . a higher irr means that the venturing activities are more attractive , while a lower irr means that they are less attractive . 
 - payback period : this is the time required for the cumulative cash inflows of the venturing activities to equal the cumulative cash outflows . it measures the breakeven point of the venturing activities , and indicates how long it takes to recover the initial investment . a shorter payback period means that the venturing activities are less risky , while a longer payback period means that they are more risky . 
 3. adjust and adapt the measurement of success and roi to the context and circumstances . the third step is to adjust and adapt the measurement of success and roi of the corporate venturing projects and programs , according to the specific context and circumstances of the venturing activities . this is important because the measurement of success and roi in corporate venturing is not a one - size - fits - all approach , but rather a dynamic and flexible process that requires constant refinement and improvement . some of the factors that may affect the measurement of success and roi in corporate venturing are : 
 - the type and stage of the venturing activities : different types and stages of venturing activities may have different objectives , metrics , methods , and tools for measuring success and roi . for example , the measurement of success and roi for an early - stage internal incubator may be different from that of a late - stage external accelerator . 
 - the industry and market of the venturing activities : different industries and markets may have different standards , benchmarks , and expectations for measuring success and roi . for example , the measurement of success and roi for a venturing activity in a mature and stable industry may be different from that of a venturing activity in a nascent and volatile industry . 
 - the culture and strategy of the company : different companies may have different cultures and strategies that influence the measurement of success and roi . for example , the measurement of success and roi for a venturing activity in a conservative and risk - averse company may be different from that of a venturing activity in a progressive and risk - taking company .

 9. best practices and lessons learned in corporate venturing 
 practices and lessons 
 practices and lessons learned 
 corporate venturing is a strategic approach to innovation that involves collaborating with external partners , such as startups , universities , or other organizations , to create new value for the corporation . corporate venturing can take various forms , such as corporate venture capital , incubators , accelerators , joint ventures , or strategic alliances . however , regardless of the form , corporate venturing projects and programs require careful design and structure to ensure alignment with the corporate strategy , objectives , and culture , as well as to manage the risks and uncertainties involved . in this section , we will discuss some of the best practices and lessons learned in corporate venturing , based on the experiences and insights of different practitioners and experts . we will cover the following topics : 
 1. how to define the scope and objectives of corporate venturing projects and programs . this involves clarifying the purpose , vision , and goals of the corporate venturing initiative , as well as the expected outcomes and metrics of success . it also involves identifying the target domains , markets , and technologies , as well as the potential partners and stakeholders . a clear and well - defined scope and objectives can help to align the corporate venturing activities with the corporate strategy and priorities , as well as to communicate the value proposition and expectations to the internal and external audiences . 
 2. how to design the governance and organizational structure of corporate venturing projects and programs . this involves determining the roles and responsibilities of the corporate venturing team , as well as the reporting and decision - making processes . it also involves defining the degree of autonomy and integration of the corporate venturing unit , as well as the level of involvement and support from the corporate leadership and functions . a well - designed governance and organizational structure can help to balance the trade - offs between control and flexibility , as well as to foster collaboration and trust among the corporate venturing actors and stakeholders . 
 3. how to select and manage the corporate venturing partners and portfolio . this involves applying the appropriate criteria and methods to screen , evaluate , and select the external partners , such as startups , universities , or other organizations , that can offer the most value and fit for the corporate venturing objectives and scope . it also involves establishing and maintaining the relationships and agreements with the partners , as well as monitoring and evaluating their performance and progress . a well - selected and managed corporate venturing portfolio can help to maximize the learning and innovation outcomes , as well as to mitigate the risks and challenges of working with external partners . 
 4. how to foster the culture and capabilities of corporate venturing within the corporation . this involves developing and nurturing the mindset , skills , and behaviors that are conducive to corporate venturing , such as curiosity , experimentation , agility , and openness . it also involves creating and leveraging the platforms , tools , and resources that can support and enable corporate venturing , such as networks , communities , events , and training . a well - fostered culture and capabilities of corporate venturing can help to enhance the engagement and motivation of the corporate venturing team and stakeholders , as well as to facilitate the knowledge transfer and value creation between the corporation and the external partners . 
 these are some of the best practices and lessons learned in corporate venturing that can help to design and structure effective and successful corporate venturing projects and programs . however , it is important to note that there is no one - size - fits - all solution for corporate venturing , as each corporation and context may have different needs and challenges . therefore , it is advisable to adopt a flexible and adaptive approach to corporate venturing , and to continuously learn and improve from the feedback and results .
