 box 11 spatial planning optimization for the cost - effectiveness of forest and landscape restoration 
 increasingly , spatial planning tools are available to maximize the benefits of restoration interventions and minimize the negative impacts of land - use decisions . the restoration opportunities assessment methodology , 247 developed by the international union for conservation of nature and the world resources institute , is a flexible cost - effective framework that can be used to identify priority areas and restoration interventions at the national and subnational levels . the we plan - forests platform , 248 created by the international institute for sustainability and the secretariat of the convention on biological diversity , helps countries identify where forest and landscape restoration can achieve the greatest biodiversity and climate benefits ; quantify trade - offs among multiple objectives of restoration ; and fully harness the potential of natural regeneration as a cost - effective restoration strategy . a study on the use of we plan - forests in six pilot countries integrated spatially explicit estimates of where natural regeneration is possible with a model of establishment and opportunity costs to create new estimates of forest restoration costs ; it demonstrated that accounting for natural regeneration in addition to active regeneration could reduce the establishment costs of forest restoration by 51 – 65 percent and create billions of us dollars in savings . 249 
 agroforestry increases biodiversity and carbon in landscapes and can increase smallholder income and resilience but requires incentives to cover risks and upfront costs 
 agroforestry is a land - use system that involves the use of perennial woody species with agricultural crops or livestock in a given space and over a given period . forty - three percent of all agricultural land globally – more than 1 billion ha – has at least 10 percent tree cover . 250 the components of agroforestry ( animals , crops and trees ) can be combined in a wide range of production processes . the three main types of agroforestry system are : ( 1 ) agro silvicultural ( trees combined with crops ) ; ( 2 ) silvopastoral ( trees combined with animals ) ; and ( 3 ) agrosilvopastoral ( trees , animals and crops ) . 
 as an integrated agrifood system , agroforestry has the potential to advance global food security by increasing crop yield and resilience , providing ecosystem services , addressing land degradation and improving livelihood resilience . 251 of the 2.2 billion ha of degraded land identified as potentially available for restoration worldwide , 1.5 billion ha is considered best - suited for mosaic restoration in which forests and trees are combined with other land uses such as agroforestry , smallholder agriculture and settlements . 252 the strategic establishment of trees on degraded land can increase agricultural productivity and the provision of ecosystem services , such as improved soil nutrient - and water - holding capacity and pest and weed management . 253 , 254 
 it is estimated that agroforestry systems can contain 50 – 80 percent of the diversity of natural forests and can have 60 percent higher mean taxa richness than forests ( consisting of both forest and non - forest species ) . 255 this higher biodiversity includes above - and below - ground flora and fauna species , many of which ( such as pollinators , soil organisms and mycorrhizae ) can increase agricultural productivity . a global meta-analysis found that restored agroecosystems , such as agroforestry systems , increase overall species diversity by an average of 68 percent and the supply of ecosystem services by 42 percent . 256 this is particularly significant for soil health , as noted in another recent meta - analysis , which found that agroforestry contributes to boosting ecosystem services , leading to a 50 percent reduction in soil erosion rates , a 21 percent increase in soil carbon storage , and a 46 percent increase in soil nitrogen availability to crops . 257 
 the measurement of tree cover on agricultural land can be used to estimate the extent of agroforestry and assess the benefits of agroforestry systems , particularly in terms of carbon sequestration . in a global analysis , remote sensing data estimated that tree cover contributed at least 75 percent of the 45.3 gtc on agricultural lands in 2010 . 258 tree cover on agricultural land increased by 3.7 percent between 2000 and 2010 , which increased carbon storage by more than 2 gtc . 259 
 given the potential of agroforestry to help mitigate and adapt to climate change , 40 percent of non - annex i countries under the unfccc propose this land use as a solution in their ndcs , with the measure embraced most widely in africa ( contained in 71 percent of ndcs ) , followed by the americas ( 34 percent of ndcs ) , asia ( 21 percent ) and oceania ( 7 percent ) ; 50 percent of the 73 developing countries with redd+ strategies have identified agroforestry as a way to combat forest decline . 260 the covid-19 pandemic has further highlighted the importance of diversified , resilient , localized production systems for maintaining animal , human and ecological health . 
 the land - equivalent ratio , defined as the ratio of the area under sole cropping to the area under intercropping needed to give equal amounts of yield at the same management level , is commonly used for comparing productivity in terms of biomass and other yields . in a study of five agroforestry systems in five european countries , the adoption of agroforestry was shown to increase agronomic productivity by 36 – 100 percent ( i . e . a land - equivalent ratio of 1 . 36 – 2 . 00 ) , depending on crop type , crop arrangement and management , and local conditions . 261 kuyah ( 2019 ) analysed 126 peer - reviewed studies on agroforestry in sub - saharan africa and concluded that , on average , agroforestry systems increased crop yield while maintaining the delivery of regulating / maintenance ecosystem services . 262 
 agroforestry is a potential option for maintaining ecological balance and diversifying rural livelihoods ( box 12 ) . 263 to date , however , it has been promoted primarily for subsistence , and many of its benefits have not been adequately quantified . the distributional ranges of both costs and benefits are highly variable , even within individual practices and systems . 
 box 12 an agroforestry model in the brazilian amazon 
 farmers in tomé-açu in the eastern amazon in brazil have developed a farmer - led agroforestry model known as safta , which combines market - oriented agroforestry systems and local agro - industry , adding value to agroforestry products and promoting exports to national and global markets . safta is a transitional agroforestry system that involves short - term annual crops , medium - term perennial crops and long - term fruit and timber tree species . 274 in the past , safta has been supported by the federal and state governments , and currently it is supported by local governments ( and it has been branded as a means to position its products in local and international markets ) . 275 although safta can take various forms , it is usually based on a combination of 1 – 3 valuable cash crops ( e . g . cocoa , cupuaçu , black pepper and açai ) and the production of oils , resins and timber . 276 
 agroforestry is a longer - term investment than conventional agriculture , requiring longer profit forecasts and planning ; 264 , 265 it can also incur high establishment and maintenance costs , sometimes generating net losses in the first few years . 266 on average , agroforestry sees profitable returns after 3 – 8 years ; for annual cropping systems , this period is normally 1 – 2 years . 
 agroforestry systems are more resilient than conventional agricultural systems to environmental shocks and the effects of climate change , such as severe storms , droughts and floods , due largely to the diversity of benefits they provide . 267 they increase food security and nutrition by serving as safety nets during such shocks , 268 especially when these affect entire communities rather than single households . 269 in an upland area of the philippines , for example , smallholder farmers who adopted agroforestry had 42 – 137 percent higher earning capacity and food security than farmers who practised annual monocropping . 270 
 despite the wide - ranging environmental benefits of agroforestry , its adoption and scaling up face challenges , many of which are socio - economic in nature , including labour , gender and farm size . 271 high establishment costs and longer - term returns , access to capital and markets , knowledge and capacity management , and land - tenure insecurity all represent significant barriers to the uptake of agroforestry by farmers . smallholder producers face trade - offs between alternative land uses , such as monocropping , and need to assess the comparative profitability of a given practice , including whether the practice is culturally appropriate . 272 although numerous studies have demonstrated the higher productivity of agroforestry systems , many farmers perceive such systems as less productive and thus financially unviable or risky . 273 
 the greater uptake of agroforestry requires effective incentives and strategic investments to achieve restoration and improved production objectives , such as providing support for tree establishment , increasing the knowledge and capacity of smallholders and extension professionals in tree - growing , and improving access to markets . 277 , 278 , 279 
 government incentives , redesigned agricultural credits and payments for ecosystem services can help address the significant barrier of limited short - term cashflow . in peru , a national policy on agroforestry concessions grants land rights to smallholders who encroached forest land before 2011 on the condition that they conserve and sustainably manage forests and establish agroforestry . 280 given adequate carbon prices and institutional support , payments for carbon sequestration may further incentivize uptake . 304 a study in ethiopia found that carbon revenue made agroforestry more profitable than monocropping , with carbon revenue being even higher than the net revenue of any monoculture plot when the sequestration rate was high and the price of carbon was at its highest . 281 
 green recovery from the pandemic is an opportunity to increase the restoration effort and thereby create jobs and enable long - term increases in land productivity 
 as of 2020 , nearly two - thirds of the usd 115 billion per year in public funds invested in nature - based solutions is being spent on restoration ( forest and peatland restoration , regenerative agriculture , water conservation and natural pollution control systems ) . 282 
 building back after the covid-19 pandemic requires not only economic growth but also supporting productive healthy ecosystems ( i . e . “ green ” recovery ) . given their potentially high economic returns , 283 the forest sector and nature - based approaches like flr , peatland rewetting and agroforestry can be effective as part of a green recovery . the potential environmental and socio - economic benefits of flr and agroforestry are immense , but so too are the challenges of planning and implementing successful interventions on the ground . thus , considerable effort is needed to compile and share data and knowledge on flr and agroforestry and how to put these into effect efficiently and to optimize the benefits .

3.title: An economic view on the costs and benefits of forest restoration | Restoring Forests and Trees for Sustainable Development: Policies, Practices, Impacts, and Ways Forward | Oxford Academic
3.content:
restoring forests and trees for sustainable development : policies , practices , impacts , and ways forward 
 chapter 
 9 
 an economic view on the costs and benefits of forest restoration 
 pablo pacheco , 
 pablo pacheco 
 craig beatty , 
 craig beatty 
 jwalin patel 
 jwalin patel 
 https : / / doi . org / 10 . 1093 / 9780197683958 . 003 . 0009 
 pages 238 – 260 
 published : september 2024 
 cite 
 pacheco , pablo , craig beatty , and jwalin patel , ' an economic view on the costs and benefits of forest restoration ' , in pia katila , and others ( eds ) , restoring forests and trees for sustainable development : policies , practices , impacts , and ways forward ( new york , ny , 2024 ; online edn , oxford academic , 6 sept. 2024 ) , https : / / doi . org / 10 . 1093 / 9780197683958 . 003 . 0009 , accessed 29 july 2025 . 
 abstract 
 this chapter focuses on assessing the costs and benefits of forest restoration . it provides key findings and knowledge gaps drawing on a review of available studies and data , assessing the costs and benefits of forest restoration across six different restoration options . it looks at both financial analysis of the costs incurred and benefits accrued by private actors or enterprises and wider economic analysis of the returns of forest restoration to society at large . it shows that while financial costs and benefits vary widely across and within forest restoration options , almost all forest restoration options are financially attractive . natural regeneration options are the least costly options , followed by tree plantations . agroforestry systems are most costly , requiring higher upfront investments , yet may yield higher economic and ecological benefits depending on the agroforestry system . there are several trade - offs associated with forest restoration , mainly regarding the financial , socioeconomic , and environmental benefits of restoration . 
 keywords : forest restoration , restoration options , costs , benefits , financial analysis , economic analysis , trade - offs 
 subject conservation of the environment ( environmental science ) applied ecology ( environmental science ) management of land and natural resources ( environmental science ) environmental sustainability environmental science 
 collection : oxford scholarship online 
 9.1 introduction 
 we are facing an unprecedented scale of nature loss due in part to the continuous process of land and forest degradation ( 
 ipbes 2018 ) . the loss of natural ecosystems leads to increasing carbon emissions that contribute to climate change and translate in diminishing ecosystem services ( 
 ipcc 2019 ) . this has raised stark concerns given the expected growing global demand for food , animal feed , and materials , which tend to rely on these services . the impacts from land and forest degradation are escalating , leading to growing calls not only to improve the efficient and sustainable use of existing land but to invest in restoring the integrity of degraded natural ecosystems , which would lead to broad financial , social , and environmental benefits ( 
 unep 2021 ) . 
 actions taken to restore ecological productivity thus far , especially in working lands and the natural ecosystems that support forest landscapes , form the basis of the initial bonn challenge . this global initiative aims to place 350 mha of degraded and deforested land under restoration by 2030 . flowing from this work and the recognition of the role that restored ecosystems can play in addressing declines in nature and human well - being , the united nations declared 2021 – 2030 the decade on ecosystem restoration . in addition , the kunming - montreal global biodiversity framework embraces the target to “ ensure that by 2030 at least 30 % of areas of degraded terrestrial , inland water , and coastal and marine ecosystems are under effective restoration , in order to enhance biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services , ecological integrity and connectivity ” ( 
 cbd 2022 , 2 ) . 
 growing support for restoration is founded on the understanding that restoring natural ecosystems , including forests , is not only critical to address biodiversity loss ( 
 ipbes 2018 ) but can also contribute to carbon removals from the atmosphere ( 
 ipcc 2019 ) . reforestation and restoration of degraded forests are considered among the most effective land - based strategies for sequestering carbon emissions to combat climate change ( 
 griscom et al. 2017 ) , and tree restoration might have positive impacts on food security ( 
 ickowitz et al. 2022 ) . such perspectives implicitly assume that restoration efforts resulting in ecosystem services recovery — including climate regulation , clean air , fresh water , and soil fertility — translate into social , economic , and financial gains ( 
 sutton et al. 2016 ) . 
 these potential gains , however , might materialize under different time horizons and might differ across places since ecological gains from restoration depend on local climate conditions ( 
 zhou et al. 2022 ) and the landscape ’s ecological context ( 
 gilby 
 et al. 2018 
 ) . in addition , depending on the social context in which restoration occurs , and the types of restoration interventions undertaken , externalities may arise . for example , forest restoration may displace agricultural activities in working lands that produce food , or may affect the livelihoods of poor landholders with insecure tenure rights . forest restoration may also affect local economies by disrupting land values and prices , leading to conflict over resources . when forest restoration leads to financial gains , it may result in inequitable distribution of the associated costs and benefits among involved stakeholders . while there is a relatively good understanding of the environmental benefits of ecosystem restoration ( 
 ipbes 2018 ) , the economic and financial gains of tree and forest restoration , as well as the potential net gains across contexts and disparate restoration options , are not well determined ( 
 bodin et al. 2021 ) . 
 this chapter focuses on forest restoration using trees , which we will refer to simply as forest restoration . it is noteworthy that forest restoration is only one of many types of restorative actions that increase ecological integrity in the farms and landscapes beyond forests ( 
 iucn and wri 2014 ) . our objective is to contribute to the discussion on economic and financial costs and benefits of trees and forest restoration across options . we do not provide an exhaustive review of available studies assessing these costs and benefits but highlight some key findings and knowledge gaps . the assessment of costs and benefits from an economic and financial perspective is undertaken through cost–bene fit analysis ( cba ) . cba consists , first , of the financial analysis of the costs incurred and benefits accrued by private actors or enterprises ( e . g . , farmers , firms , investors ) undertaking restoration and , second , of the wider economic analysis of the returns of forest restoration to society at large . financial analyses measure the financial performance of a particular restoration activity but do not consider externalities . economic analyses involve comprehensive cost and benefit assessments for the whole society and tend to include the monetary value of ecosystem services , which is estimated based on their market value if they have one ; otherwise it is estimated using different valuation methods . these assessments increasingly rely on spatially explicit analysis to better capture the spatial dimension of environmental services ’ provision , which tends to differ across places depending on the ecosystems currently under analysis . 
 the costs of forest restoration include not only short - to mid - term direct costs to establish and maintain trees and forests but also transaction costs , opportunity costs , and external costs . in turn , the benefits of forest restoration are associated with direct benefits to employment and income generated by restoration actions , as well as the incremental benefits from the recovery of forest ecosystem services to people , which are typically classified as provisioning , regulating , supporting , and cultural services . the most common forest restoration options ( also known as interventions , actions , techniques , modalities , or systems ) comprise natural regeneration under passive and assisted modalities , agroforestry , agrosilvopastoral systems , and tree plantations and woodlots ( 
 iucn and wri 2014 ) . these restoration options may occur in lands under different management regimes including public lands , community lands and territories , and individual landholdings ; many combinations may occur depending on the context , who initiates and performs the restoration actions , and the scale . 
 forest restoration takes place within diverse ecological , social , economic , and institutional contexts and across landscapes in different states of degradation . as such , the costs and benefits of forest restoration vary widely . given the lack of consistent methodologies and comparable data , it is difficult to determine the factors across all contexts that explain this variation ( 
 cook et al. 2017 ) . this limits our ability to make evidence - informed selections of restoration actions that are more likely to perform financially , and that yield economic and environmental returns that better serve the context needs . previous work has highlighted the lack of meaningful data on restoration costs ( 
 teeb 2010 ) . calls have been made to improve the ways in which economic data is gathered and compared across contexts ; this requires adopting common frameworks for data collection and analysis ( 
 bodin et al. 2021 ) . 
 our analysis here relies on a review of several studies focusing on the economic cba of forest restoration , complemented by six country studies including detailed financial cba with comparable data of 41 cases of forest restoration . our analysis is not exempt from the limitations of representation described above . we focus on general trends and knowledge gaps arising from the challenges of cba with a particular emphasis on forest restoration options , making necessary caveats linked to the data as explicitly as possible in our analysis and discussion . 
 understanding the costs and benefits of different forest restoration options is critical for guiding investments and designing incentives that meet social and ecological objectives under diverse social , institutional , and biophysical conditions informed by the best available knowledge . the main issues to consider when weighing different forest restoration options are their financial , socioeconomic , and environmental benefits ; how to balance short - and long - term costs and benefits ; and the distribution of costs and benefits among stakeholders to ensure equity in access to benefits . these issues must be assessed within the local context , embracing the perspectives of all relevant stakeholders , particularly indigenous peoples and local communities , smallholders , farmers , and other diverse forest users who make a living on , or whose businesses depend on , the sustainable management of land and forest resources . 
 erbaugh et al. ( 2020 ) estimate that 294 . 5 million people live on tropical forest land identified as having restoration opportunities ; thus a look at the costs and benefits of restoration should take wider social and economic considerations seriously . 
 this chapter is organized in five sections including this introduction . 
 section 2 provides elements for understanding the full range of costs and benefits associated with trees and forest restoration . 
 section 3 examines both financial and economic cba of forest restoration . the fourth section discusses factors that influence the variability of costs and benefits across and within different forest restoration options , the resulting trade - offs , and ways to deal with these trade - offs . and 
 section 4 pulls together this chapter ’s main conclusions . 
 9.2 costs and benefits of forest restoration 
 despite costs being a major concern about restoration , it is inappropriate to look at them without considering potential benefits . the costs and benefits of forest restoration are multiple and include two dimensions , private and social . private costs are 
 figure 9.1 provides a simplified description of the costs and benefits of forest restoration . the upper side consists of the full range of ( four ) categories of costs , and the lower side includes the full range of ( five ) categories of benefits . the central portion of the diagram depicts the scales at which forest restoration can occur , either at the farm and/or land management unit ( or groups of them ) or at the whole landscape scale , the latter delineated by either ecological or administrative boundaries at the subnational , national , or even regional level . 
 we identify six main forest restoration options : 1 ) natural forest regeneration , 2 ) assisted natural forest regeneration , 3 ) agroforestry with annual and/or perennial crops , 4 ) agrosilvopastoral systems , 5 ) tree plantations with annual crops , and 6 ) tree plantations in monocrops . these six options are included in 
 figure 9.1 and outlined in detail in 
 appendix 9 a . furthermore , context - specific factors , such as those related to ecological conditions , political economies , and cultures , not only influence which options are undertaken but also the associated costs and benefits of the different restoration options at either the farm and land management units — depending on the land ownership and management type — or landscape levels . 
 figure 9.1 
 private and social costs and benefits of forest restoration ( source : authors ’ own depiction ) 
 restoration costs include the direct costs that correspond not only to the initial investments for undertaking physical restoration activities but also the operational expenses incurred for long - term tree , tree - crop , and forest management . direct costs are a function of the biophysical conditions where forest restoration takes place , in that poorer biophysical conditions will tend to either increase the scope of initial restoration investment or extend the timeline over which restoration takes place ( e . g . , soil quality and water availability ) . as a result , the greater the degradation , the higher the cost . 
 forest restoration is nested within institutional processes aimed at planning , providing access to information , generating social and group incentives for action , enabling participation , and building capacity for long - term sustainable management ( 
 verdone 2015 ) . these constitute enabling conditions shaping the outcomes of forest restoration . these conditions entail transaction costs , which are seldom documented systematically ( 
 bodin et al. 2021 ) . these costs are strongly influenced by context - specific conditions associated with not only biophysical factors of the landscapes where restoration takes place but also socio - institutional characteristics of the groups undertaking forest restoration . these conditions vary depending on the scale at which restoration actions are undertaken . 
 in addition , opportunity costs and external costs are two types of costs that should be considered in planning and evaluating forest restoration . opportunity costs of restoration consist of the foregone economic benefits of alternative land - use choices where restoration takes place ( 
 verdone 2015 ) . most typical alternative land uses to forest restoration are those linked to non - forest land uses , such as commercial agriculture and livestock production . land - use choices depend not only on land suitability but also on availability of labor and access to capital and inputs ( 
 barbier 2007 ) . 
 external costs , when taking a wider social perspective , are those costs generated by the externalities of restoration . these costs are borne by society at large , beyond the 
 private costs of farmers , landowners , or firms conducting restoration . the external costs differ depending on the restoration option and scale ( 
 hebling 2010 ) , and social externalities may occur . for example , tree plantations could demand a large supply of water , or tree planting may compete with productive agricultural land , thereby affecting the supply of food . restoration through monoculture plantations may exclude local populations from the benefits of restoration or restrict them access to land that is critical for their livelihoods . 
 the benefits of forest restoration consist of the incremental socioeconomic and environmental gains when compared with a degradation baseline . the socioeconomic benefits from restoration often translate into jobs and employment , safety nets , and livelihood diversification for landholders undertaking restoration . in addition , the commonly used typology of forest ecosystem services to people has four additional categories of benefits : provisioning services ( e . g . , food supply , timber , fiber , medicines , energy ) , regulating services ( e . g . , water regulation , climate regulation , disease and pest regulation , pollination ) , supporting services ( e . g . , nutrient cycling , photosynthesis , soil formation ) , and cultural services ( e . g . , enriching , spiritual and religious , recreation , aesthetics ) ( 
 mea 2005 ) . in this classification there is no explicit mention of biodiversity , yet biodiversity can be considered a fundamental supporting service that underpins the delivery of all other services ( 
 oecd 2018 ) . 
 many of the benefits from forest restoration take time to accrue , except for some financial gains from annual crop production and income for labor invested in restoration activities . for example , annual crops intercropped with perennial crops generate returns in shorter timeframes compared with timber for logging , depending on the tree species planted . in addition , social benefits from restoration , such as improved safety nets or social resilience accrue over longer timeframes . this is the case of environmental benefits as well , including regulating services ( e . g . , climate and water regulation , erosion control ) and supporting services ( e . g . , nutrient cycling ) . while some benefits of forest restoration accrue directly to farmers and firms , particularly provisioning services , several benefits are not confined to restoration lands and involve more distant climatic and ecological interactions . 
 the six forest restoration options vary in the socioeconomic and environmental benefits they generate . options oriented to improve provisioning services , including the production of monetizable goods such as crops , timber , fuel wood , and non - timber forest products , will deliver greater private economic benefits . proximity to markets and the mix of goods , which is also linked to the tree species selected for restoration , can determine on what scale and over what timespan forest restoration benefits materialize . options that are more labor - intensive are expected to generate additional jobs and income , though the quality of those jobs may vary ( 
 raes et al. 2021 ) . options such as agroforestry , agrosilvopastoral systems , and tree plantations with crops can contribute to income generation and livelihood diversification for local farmers , with the potential to satisfy social needs ( e . g . , health , education ) ( 
 raes et al. 2017 ; sunderland and rowland 2019 ) . 
 furthermore , natural regeneration leads to greater environmental benefits through carbon capture , recovery of biodiversity , and water regulation — benefits that accumulate when lower - cost forest restoration allows implementation at larger spatial scales ( 
 chazdon and uriarte 2016 ; 
 crouzeilles et al. 2020 ) . the potential environmental 
 benefits of agroforestry are extensive , including soil fertility recovery , soil salinity control , erosion reduction , water quality improvement , and biodiversity and pollinator habitat protection and recovery . restoration interventions designed to satisfy fuelwood supply may reduce pressures on natural forests ( 
 montagnini 2017 ; 
 raes et al. 2017 ) . there is a diversity of agroforestry systems ; the precise array of benefits depends on the system under consideration , its site characteristics , local economies , and management approaches . monoculture plantations , instead , may contribute to higher impacts on carbon sequestration ( 
 bernal et al. 2018 ) yet have limited or negative impacts on nature ( 
 albert et al. 2021 ) and use excessive amounts of water ( 
 vanclay 2009 ) . 
 context - specific factors , including the local biophysical settings and the state of degradation of the land and forest where restoration takes place , influence the costs incurred in forest restoration activities . restoration outcomes , and the benefits they deliver , are influenced by the speed of ecological recovery , which can depend on climate stress and biotic agents ( 
 jones et al. 2018 ) , percentage of forest cover ( 
 arroyo - rodríguez et al. 2023 ) , temperature and precipitation conditions ( 
 zhou et al. 2022 ) , and others factors including variability in soil type , density and depth , and drainage conditions . soil recovery is a critical ingredient of successful ecosystem restoration ( 
 van der sande et al. 2023 ) . political economy factors — including infrastructure , market development , price distortions , and resource competition — impact the costs of land , labor , and inputs , thereby influencing restoration costs . furthermore , cultural systems , including values toward and conceptualizations of nature , may influence locally desired forest restoration options , acknowledging that diverse cultural values may coexist in landscapes ( 
 schultz et al. 2022 ) . 
 9.3 economic and financial costs and benefits 
 the most common approach for assessing the private and social gains from forest restoration actions is cba . typical cba can be conducted from a wider social perspective by considering the costs and benefits for society at large or from a purely private perspective to evaluate the financial profitability of the investments . while the latter may also have wider socio - environmental implications , these are often omitted from financial analysis ( 
 campbell and brown 2012 ) . when looking at cba for restoration , financial cba helps to understand the net financial gains across restoration options from a private perspective for farms , firms , and investors , with limited or no consideration of externalities or social costs of these activities . in turn , cbas that include whole landscapes or wider administrative jurisdictions ( e . g . , countries , states , provinces ) require adopting a social perspective , accounting for economic costs and benefits to society , such as net changes in ecosystem services . this expands the cba scope to include public goods not only with a monetary value but also with a nonmonetary value . economic analyses tend to group these services in use values and nonuse values or those that are more intangible . several methods are applied to conduct the economic valuation used in ecosystem services valuation but not without challenges ( 
 oecd 2018 ) . 
 table 9.1 shows the differences between economic and financial cost–bene fit approaches . see also 
 wainaina et al. ( 2020 ) for a more detailed explanation of these differences .

 9.3.1 
 economic cost–bene fit analyses 
 economic cba of restoration is used to determine the net returns from reversing land degradation , which is typically categorized as leading to significant social and economic benefits . land degradation is an incremental process that is estimated to have affected around 75 % of the global land surface , including forests ( 
 ipbes 2019 ) . some estimate the global impact of deforestation and deteriorating agricultural productivity at about usd 6.3 trillion per year , arising from the loss of ecosystem services including climate regulation , clean air , fresh water , and soil fertility ( 
 sutton et al. 2016 ) . adverse socioeconomic outcomes linked to land degradation include the loss of livelihoods and land productivity ( 
 barbier and hochard 2018 ) . land degradation also affects a range of cultural elements arising from community interactions with nature that give meaning to life and contribute to well - being ( 
 reyes - garcía et al. 2013 ) . indeed , climate change and the looming biodiversity crisis reflect the consequences of the long and well - examined history of human - driven nature and habitat loss . 
 several global comparative reviews have been undertaken to understand the economic costs and benefits of ecosystem restoration . for example , 
 de groot et al. ( 2013 ) , reviews 94 studies of costs and 225 studies of benefits associated with ecosystem restoration projects across nine different biomes . while acknowledging data limitations and static estimates , he argues that the majority of restoration projects analyzed have provided net benefits and should be considered profitable . in this analysis , costs include capital investment and maintenance of restoration interventions , and benefits correspond to the total monetary value of the ecosystem services 
 provided by the restored ecosystem . when looking at tropical forests ( 96 estimates ) , the total economic value ( tev ) of all services equals usd 5 , 264 / ha ( sd = 6 , 526 ) , with usd 1 , 588 / ha ( sd = 317 ) for woodlands . the tev of forest - related restoration is lower compared with those in coral reefs and coastal wetlands . the analysis on monetary values builds upon 
 de groot et al. ’s ( 2012 ) study that estimated values for 22 ecosystem services . this analysis , however , is not exempt from issues , among others , such as data heterogeneity , monetary estimate generalization for context - specific environmental services , value transference across socioeconomic contexts , as well as value estimate selection bias . 
 a systematic review of cba conducted by wainaina et . al. ( 
 2020 ) based on 31 articles across latin america , southeast asia , and sub - saharan africa finds that most papers conducting economic cba ( 84 % ) rely on estimates of use values ( direct and indirect ) ( e . g . , erosion control , air regulation , temperature regulation , recreational value , avoided nutrient loss , nitrogen fixation , and soil fertility improvement ) , and only a few include nonuse values ( e . g . , aesthetic value , bequest ( inheritance ) values , existence value ) . this analysis shows that most of the cases analyzed report positive net present values ( npv s ) for the different restoration options considered ( i . e . , agroforestry , soil and water conservation , mangrove restoration ) . however , the number of studies that report positive npvs for reforestation and afforestation is equal to the ones that report negative npv s . for other options ( i . e . , assisted natural regeneration ( anr ) , woodlot establishment ) , the number of studies that report positive npvs is higher than the number that report negative npv s . 
 wainaina et al. ( 2020 ) highlight that the different studies assessed use different methods to valuate the respective benefits . there is an increasing use of spatial analysis for determining some environmental values , including net carbon sequestration . a few studies also apply contingent valuation methods for benefits , for example , of air pollution and recreational values . 
 birch et al. ( 2010 ) assess the cost - effectiveness of dryland forest restoration using spatial analysis of ecosystem services in four study areas in latin america . this study estimates the npvs of carbon sequestration , non - timber forest products , timber , tourism , and livestock production . the cost - effectiveness of restoration is analyzed by estimating the net social benefit of restoration . the study finds that passive natural restoration is a cost - effective option , while the benefits from active restoration are outweighed by the relatively higher costs involved . this is likely due to the higher opportunity costs associated with the loss of income from livestock production — the main alternative land use in the study areas — and that only a few environmental benefits are considered . similarly , 
 newton et al. ( 2012 ) , assessing the cost–benefits of ecological networks based on a case in dorset , england , argue that establishing these networks in landscapes dominated by agricultural land uses may not deliver net economic benefits given relatively higher land - use opportunity costs . 
 9.3.2 financial cost–bene fit analyses 
 there is a growing number of studies analyzing the financial performance for private farms , firms , and investors by conducting cba of specific forest restoration options . 
 247 table 9.2 presents data on financial costs and benefit - cost ratios ( cbr ) across tree and forest restoration options for 41 different cases originating from six country studies . these studies were conducted by the international union for conservation of nature ( iucn ) and the world resources institute ( wri ) using the restoration opportunities assessment methodology ( roam ) at national and subnational jurisdictional scales ( 
 iucn and wri 2014 ) . in the roam studies , costs and benefits are estimated through financial cba at the country or landscape level , and some conduct multi - criteria analysis ( mca ) including the spatially explicit optimization of economic outcomes across multiple objectives , including the provision of ecosystem services , under different social and biophysical constraints ( 
 beatty et al. 2018a ; 
 robbins and daniels 2012 ) . some of these studies consist of cba estimates for a time horizon of 20 years , while others comprise 30 years . most of these estimates calculate npv using a 10 % discount rate . to facilitate comparison , estimates are adjusted for inflation in their respective currencies to 2020 , and then converted to 2020 usd . the extent of comparability of these figures is subject to the comparability of the contexts and objectives of restoration in each place .

( 2017 ) for el salvador . na = not available because they were not assessed in the studies reviewed , which does not mean that those options do not deliver benefits across those categories as well . the benefits included in the table are all those that were included in the studies reviewed . 
 overall , these estimates suggest that forest restoration options with the lowest financial costs are those linked to the natural regeneration of forests ; costs are somewhat higher when assisted practices are used compared to passive natural forest regeneration . restoration using monoculture plantations or woodlots have relatively higher short - term direct costs than natural regeneration , but lower than other options . natural regeneration and tree plantations are likely implemented at larger spatial scales than agroforestry or agrosilvopastoral approaches and , thus , are likely to benefit from economies of scale , while the latter two have higher short - and long - term direct costs . the options with the highest short - term direct costs involve agroforestry , particularly when including high - value tree crops such as cacao . these estimates , however , would be lower when restoration actions aim at enhancing existing systems , including agro - successional systems ( 
 vieira et al. 2009 ) , rather than establishing new ones . 
 in line with our findings , a study focusing on agroforestry systems in latin america suggests that agroforestry systems are profitable in most cases ( 
 current et al. 1995 ) . the study finds that agroforestry , which includes intercropping with perennials , perform better , as it diversifies income , adds value per unit of land , and improves cash streams . in addition , an analysis of restoration costs in brazil , comprising the amazon , cerrado , and atlantic forest biomes , suggests that passive and anr are comparatively cheaper ( usd 48 / ha and usd 344 / ha , respectively ) but are used less since most restoration interventions use seedling planting and direct seeding that are more costly ( usd 2 , 328 / ha and usd 1 , 754 / ha , respectively ) , with a larger portion of the tree planting costs incurred during the implementation phase ( 
 brancalion et al. 2019 ) . the authors suggest that these costs depend on local market conditions , among other factors . 
 the financial cba estimates encompass only the direct monetary costs and benefits to farms , firms , and investors and opportunity costs of the foregone financial benefits from likely alternative land uses . for comparison , we present bcr to provide an indication of the performance of expected financial benefits over costs . bcr are greater than one in most of the cases , with a few exceptions , which suggests that 
 the financial benefits exceed their cost counterparts across most of the restoration options . it is hard to generalize in terms of bcr within specific response options or across them since they can be influenced by the specificity of countries and contexts , and there are no observable patterns across options based on the information shown in 
 table 9 . 2 . moreover , as each case constitutes an average estimate for that specific option in each country , it is not possible to observe the variation in costs within each country , which limits a meaningful comparison of how these different bcrs perform with each other or the factors explaining the variations . it is noteworthy that bcrs do not provide complete information on the feasibility of any restoration option in particular ; this is because the “ success ” of a restoration activity or project should be interpreted contextually in line with restoration objectives , motivation , the time horizon over which benefits accrue , how are they distributed and to whom , and implementation experience that go beyond financial metrics . 
 9.3.3 social and environmental benefits 
 the six tree and forest restoration options , beyond their disparate financial profitability , each tend to deliver differing benefits depending on specific socio - ecological conditions , as already mentioned , which merit consideration . as part of wider economic assessments of restoration , some roam studies have also conducted analysis — although in a less systematic way — of the likely social and environmental benefits of tree and forest restoration interventions , particularly those that can be more easily assessed due to available estimates and existing prediction models . some of these rely on average national estimates , yet others draw on spatially explicit modeling outcomes such as erosion and nutrient exports . 
 table 9.2 compares the expected socioeconomic and environmental benefits associated with six tree and forest restoration options from our review of six roam country studies . 
 the previous comparison suggests that all forest restoration options have the potential to generate positive socioeconomic and environmental impacts in the right circumstances , though these impacts differ depending on the restoration option , as well as context - specific conditions ( e . g . , establishment location , management system , site productivity ) . for example , natural forest regeneration options tend to have more long - term environmental benefits than direct short - term economic gains , since their most common purpose is to restore missing or degraded environmental functions that result from forest loss or degradation . in addition , while plantations may deliver short - term economic benefits and contribute to carbon removal and erosion reduction , their impacts on biodiversity are questionable ( 
 wang et al. 2022 ) . yet , benefits from plantations also depend on the choice of crops when combined with annual crops . furthermore , agroforestry systems — including intercropping of trees , high - value trees , and annual crops — deliver important short - term benefits derived from jobs as well as long - term economic benefits from fuelwood and food supply , and environmental benefits through reversing soil erosion and enhancing sediment retention , if managed appropriately ( see 
 fao 2017 ) . 
 different restoration options often deliver multiple benefits simultaneously ( monetary and nonmonetary ) at the farm or land management units and landscape scales . using mca has become a common approach to analyzing financial , socioeconomic , 
 and environmental indicators altogether , particularly to support restoration planning while considering different social and biophysical constraints , under the understanding that it may improve the cost - effectiveness of restoration investments ( 
 beatty et al. 2018a ; 
 robbins and daniels 2012 ) . for example , 
 strassburg et al. ( 2019 ) argue that strategic approaches to ecosystem restoration , while considering spatial socio - environmental constraints and opportunities , can triple conservation gains and halve the costs ; the increase in benefits results from compromise solutions that simultaneously deliver the maximum outcome for both biodiversity conservation and carbon sequestration , and the reduction in costs is associated with efficiencies of scale and the prioritization of areas with lower opportunity costs . 
 9.4 discussion 
 forest restoration and increased tree cover are acknowledged as promising options to deliver social , economic , and environmental benefits ( 
 iucn and wri 2014 ) . as our analysis shows , in line with what others have determined ( see 
 strassburg and latawiec 2014 ) , in many circumstances and locations , forest restoration benefits outweigh the costs involved in the establishment and management of trees ; yet those benefits depend on what forest restoration options are adopted and by whom . the establishment and management of trees — sometimes in combination with crops — under different forest restoration options differ across places and their diverse social , biological , and geographic conditions . there are many contextual factors that influence the private and social costs and benefits of forest restoration efforts and whether these efforts lead to successful outcomes in the long run ( 
 mansourian et al. 2021 ) . in addition , forest restoration is always associated with socio - environmental trade - offs , depending on the objectives and the timeframes in which benefits materialize . thus , the costs and benefits of forest restoration activities can be better understood by taking into consideration the disparity of costs and benefits across options , their likely trade - offs under different time horizons , and the contextual factors shaping outcomes from the farm to the landscape . 
 9.4.1 disparity of costs and benefits 
 significant disparities across forest restoration options are found in the financial costs and benefit analysis , from a private perspective , for the actors ( e . g . , farms , firms , investors ) who undertake forest restoration . overall , costs seem to rise with increasing complexity of the option adopted in terms of active tree planting , combination of trees , requirements of labor and inputs , and the associated management ; these costs are also distributed over time . for example , restoration options favoring natural regeneration are the less costly option , followed by anr . moreover , the options that require lower establishment and management costs ( e . g . , monoculture timber plantations or woodlots ) demand lower costs than more complex systems ( e . g . , agroforestry including different combinations of trees , and perennial and annual crops ) . some options like agroforestry require higher upfront investments for establishment ; yet , as demonstrated by those cases where there is a large use of perennial crops ( e . g . , cacao , coffee , 
 banana ) , the expectation to obtain higher benefits can be a strong incentive for adopting these systems . however , it is likely that the objectives of restoration will limit the available restoration options , leaving decision - making as less of a process of selecting from a large number of types and more toward the specific considerations within a small subset of restoration options that deliver on the selected restoration objectives . 
 while the total costs vary across options depending on the labor , inputs , and materials that are employed , they are also influenced by the previous land use under which restoration takes place . in this regard , evidence from a meta-analysis suggests ecological recovery from landscape restoration is more successful on land regimes with less intensive previous disturbance ( 
 crouzeilles et al. 2016 ) . in general , restoration activities aimed at enhancing the environmental and economic performance of preexisting systems may demand lower financial investment and establishment costs compared to those entailing more drastic shifts in land use . nonetheless , additional restorative actions may be needed in intervened working lands where farmers depend on their land for their livelihoods . thus , restoration options that deliver subsistence and commercial gains may be preferred despite their relatively higher costs . furthermore , economies of scale ( i . e . , reductions in the average cost of restoration as area is increased ) are unlikely to arise in most forest restoration options . possible exceptions include production forestry , where the dominant practice of monoculture tree plantations may allow easier planting and harvesting cycles that meet the expected financial returns , subject to site productivity . 
 forest restoration also results in wider costs and benefits for the society at large , as evidenced by economic cba . here too , significant disparities are found across restoration options . however , these disparities arise due to both methodological and restoration - based , context - driven reasons . available studies differ in the range of benefits from environmental services that are considered in analysis . additionally , results vary based on the valuation methods employed . in general , when a larger number of environmental services are monetized , analyses suggest that most restoration actions deliver net benefits to society . however , these analyses should be considered carefully , given the uncertainty in estimates . valuation methods informed by data that are not spatially relevant and reflective of local ecological conditions may generate misleading estimates of the impact of restoration on ecosystem services . furthermore , it is not entirely clear to what extent the varying positive or negative net gains from forest restoration are associated with the type of environmental services valued or with the differences across the biophysical and ecological contexts of restoration landscapes . 
 economic externalities from forest restoration options tend to receive less attention . for example , demand for water is expected from new tree plantations , which may impose externalities on irrigated agriculture and wetlands , depending on the context ( 
 nordblom et al. 2012 ) . forest restoration , mainly large - scale tree planting , could result in the displacement of agricultural lands , thus affecting food security ( 
 ipcc 2019 ) , which may eventually lead to growing pressures on indigenous peoples and local community lands . these impacts may be further pronounced if investments in tree plantations neglect local people ’s rights or do not meaningfully engage stakeholders . negative impacts must be avoided when planning restoration actions ; social safeguards that support rather than erode the rights and tenure of indigenous people and local communities should not be negotiable . socio - ecological gains from restoration 
 will be inextricably linked to the strengthening of local organizations , capacities , and improvements in local livelihoods , among others ( 
 erbaugh et al. 2020 ) . 
 9.4.2 trade - offs , time horizons , and uptake 
 a common trade-off in forest restoration is between the economic benefits and the environmental benefits , which also have a temporal dimension associated with the timeframes in which these benefits accrue . how economically attractive an option is should depend on the overall benefits for society , including the incremental monetary and nonmonetary benefits on ecosystem provisioning , regulating , supporting , and cultural services . overall , there is a net gain from restoration for society when a larger number of environmental benefits are valued during this comparison

4.title: Reforestation Economics 101
4.content:
reforestation economics 101 
 understanding the financial aspects of environmental restoration 
 sarah lee ai generated llama - 4 - maverick - 17 b - 128 e - instruct - fp 8 5 min read · june 17 , 2025 
 photo by ün liu on unsplash 
 introduction to reforestation economics 
 reforestation , the process of replanting trees in areas where forests have been degraded or cleared , has gained significant attention in recent years due to its potential to mitigate climate change , conserve biodiversity , and provide various ecosystem services . the economic significance of reforestation cannot be overstated , as it involves substantial investments and returns that impact local and global economies . in this article , we will explore the economic benefits and challenges of reforestation efforts in the context of environmental economics . 
 historical context of reforestation efforts 
 historically , reforestation efforts have been driven by a mix of environmental , social , and economic motivations . early reforestation initiatives were often focused on restoring degraded lands for timber production and soil conservation . however , with the growing awareness of climate change and its impacts , reforestation has become increasingly recognized as a critical strategy for carbon sequestration . the 2010s saw a significant surge in global reforestation efforts , with initiatives such as the trillion tree campaign gaining international attention . 
 importance of economic analysis in reforestation 
 economic analysis plays a crucial role in understanding the viability and impact of reforestation efforts . by evaluating the costs and benefits of reforestation , policymakers and investors can make informed decisions about resource allocation and project design . economic analysis can help identify the most cost - effective strategies for achieving reforestation goals , as well as potential barriers to implementation . 
 costs and benefits of reforestation 
 reforestation involves a range of costs and benefits that must be carefully considered in economic analyses . 
 direct costs 
 the direct costs of reforestation include : 
 land acquisition : the cost of purchasing or leasing land for reforestation . 
 seedling production : the cost of producing or purchasing tree seedlings . 
 planting : the labor and equipment costs associated with planting trees . 
 these costs can vary significantly depending on factors such as location , tree species , and labor costs . for example , a study in the amazon rainforest estimated the cost of reforestation at approximately $ 1 , 500 per hectare [ ^ 1 ] ( https : / / www . sciencedirect . com / science / article / pii / b 9780128121283000135 ) . 
 indirect costs 
 in addition to direct costs , reforestation also involves indirect costs , including : 
 opportunity costs : the value of alternative land uses that are forgone as a result of reforestation . 
 maintenance : the ongoing costs of maintaining reforested areas , including activities such as thinning and pruning . 
 opportunity costs can be significant , particularly in areas with high agricultural productivity or other competing land uses . for example , a study in indonesia estimated that the opportunity costs of reforestation could be as high as $ 1 , 000 per hectare per year [ ^ 2 ] ( https : / / www . sciencedirect . com / science / article / pii / s 0921800916302594 ) . 
 benefits 
 reforestation provides a range of benefits , including : 
 carbon sequestration : reforested areas can act as carbon sinks , mitigating climate change . 
 biodiversity conservation : reforestation can help restore habitats for threatened and endangered species . 
 ecosystem services : reforested areas can provide a range of ecosystem services , including water filtration , soil conservation , and recreation opportunities . 
 the benefits of reforestation can be substantial , with one study estimating that global reforestation efforts could generate up to $ 170 billion in annual benefits by 2050 [ ^ 3 ] ( https : / / www . ipcc . ch / sr ccl / chapter / spm / ) . 
 the following diagram illustrates the costs and benefits of reforestation :

 funding mechanisms for reforestation 
 reforestation efforts require significant funding , which can be sourced from a variety of mechanisms . 
 government grants and subsidies 
 government grants and subsidies are a common source of funding for reforestation efforts . these can take the form of direct payments to landowners or funding for reforestation projects . for example , the us government 's conservation reserve program provides financial incentives to landowners to establish reforested areas on marginal lands . 
 private investment 
 private investment is increasingly playing a key role in funding reforestation efforts . this can take the form of : 
 carbon credits : reforestation projects can generate carbon credits , which can be sold to companies and individuals looking to offset their carbon emissions . 
 impact investing : investors are increasingly looking to invest in reforestation projects that provide both financial returns and environmental benefits . 
 community - based funding models 
 community - based funding models involve local communities in the funding and management of reforestation efforts . these models can be effective in ensuring that reforestation efforts are tailored to local needs and priorities . for example , community - led reforestation initiatives in nepal have been successful in restoring degraded forests and providing benefits to local communities 1 ( https : / / www . sciencedirect . com / science / article / pii / s 0921800917300565 ) . 
 policy frameworks supporting reforestation 
 effective policy frameworks are critical to supporting reforestation efforts . 
 national and international policies 
 national and international policies can play a key role in promoting reforestation . for example , the paris agreement includes provisions related to forest conservation and restoration , while national governments can implement policies such as tax incentives for reforestation . 
 regulatory frameworks 
 regulatory frameworks , including laws and regulations , can help ensure that reforestation efforts are carried out in a sustainable and responsible manner . for example , regulations can require reforestation projects to undergo environmental impact assessments and to adhere to certain standards for tree species and planting practices . 
 incentives for sustainable land - use practices 
 incentives for sustainable land - use practices can help encourage landowners to adopt reforestation and other conservation practices . these can take the form of financial incentives , such as payments for ecosystem services , or non - financial incentives , such as certification programs for sustainably managed forests . 
 the following table summarizes the key policy frameworks supporting reforestation : 
 policy framework description 
 national and international policies promote reforestation through agreements and national policies 
 regulatory frameworks ensure reforestation is carried out sustainably and responsibly 
 incentives for sustainable land - use practices encourage landowners to adopt reforestation and conservation practices 
 conclusion 
 reforestation economics is a complex and multifaceted field that involves understanding the costs and benefits of reforestation efforts . by analyzing the economic significance of reforestation , policymakers and investors can make informed decisions about resource allocation and project design . effective policy frameworks and funding mechanisms are critical to supporting reforestation efforts and achieving their environmental and economic benefits .

 the main costs associated with reforestation include land acquisition , seedling production , planting , opportunity costs , and maintenance . 
 what are the benefits of reforestation ? 
 the benefits of reforestation include carbon sequestration , biodiversity conservation , and ecosystem services . 
 how can reforestation efforts be funded ? 
 reforestation efforts can be funded through government grants and subsidies , private investment , and community - based funding models . 
 what policy frameworks support reforestation ? 
 policy frameworks that support reforestation include national and international policies , regulatory frameworks , and incentives for sustainable land - use practices .
